archetype.name: Game Manager (efficient spot starter)
archetype.definition: A veteran backup who keeps Seattle's run-leaning, defense-first plan on schedule with on-time, mostly short throws, takes the occasional deep shot to Jaxon Smith-Njigba, and has turned the ball over almost never through the air.

report.headline: Best efficiency of his career, built on soft defenses and nine deep balls
report.take:
Drew Lock has been one of the most efficient passers in the league in his relief and spot-start work. His 0.321 EPA per dropback ranks 2nd of 54 qualifiers, against a league average of -0.021. He also ranks 2nd in yards per attempt (9.0), has completed 73.1% with a +6.24 CPOE, and has thrown no interceptions. He has done it inside a tight box. Seattle passes 6.9 points less often than situation predicts (29th), his volume sits around 23 attempts a game, and his average throw lands about a yard short of the sticks. This is a backup asked to keep the chains moving for a top-five defense, and so far he has done more than that.

The engine is narrow. Jaxon Smith-Njigba has drawn 41 of his targets for 30.4 EPA, close to the whole passing profit on his own. The depth splits tell the same story: nine attempts of 20+ air yards produced 18.9 EPA (2.099 per play) and three touchdowns, while his 44 short throws carried a respectable 0.343 per play. Throws over the middle (5 TDs, 19.1 EPA) are where the damage gets done. A clean pocket helped too. He has been pressured on just 12.6% of dropbacks, 2nd-lowest among charted passers.

What the numbers hide is the schedule and the history. His logged games came against Arizona twice (31st in defensive EPA today), Las Vegas (28th) and New England (24th). He has not been tested by a good defense. His career says something very different from this season. He has never posted an EPA per play above 0.104, and his CPOE has been negative every year, including -6.1 with the Giants in 2024. A nine-attempt deep sample and a 41-target dependence on one receiver are exactly the kind of thing that cools off. The one real crack is ball security: he lost two fumbles at Las Vegas in a game where he was sacked three times behind a line missing its tackles.

Where it heads depends mostly on a decision that isn't his. Sam Darnold is out with a quadriceps injury but listed for a return after the bye. Mike Macdonald is "really optimistic" Darnold starts against the 49ers, and Lock is back to QB2 on the depth chart. Lock is a useful, steady insurance policy. He is not a passer whose small-sample numbers should be read as a new level.

strengths.title: Interception-free, on-schedule passing
strengths.body: He has zero interceptions on 93 attempts, the best rate in the league. He has completed 73.1% (3rd) by keeping the ball short of the sticks and throwing into a run-first structure. That is partly the role: low volume, favorable scripts and soft opponents. It is also a real departure from the 15-interception 2020 version of him. Expect some interceptions to come with more volume, but the conservative approach should hold.

strengths.title: Deep connection over the middle
strengths.body: His nine deep attempts have been devastating: 2.099 EPA per play and three touchdowns. The middle of the field holds five of his seven scores. Most of it runs through Smith-Njigba, whose 0.741 EPA per target makes the shot plays work. The skill to throw the ball down the field has always been there. The rate is a nine-throw sample and will not last at this level.

strengths.title: Third-down conversion
strengths.body: On third down he has converted 50% with an average of 7.4 yards to go. That comes to 0.533 EPA per play and four touchdowns. Willingness to push the ball past the sticks on the money downs is what separates this year from his Denver tape. Thirty-two plays is enough to call it a hint rather than noise.

concerns.title: Career says regression is coming
concerns.body: Every prior season he graded at or below average. He has posted a negative CPOE each year, and in 2024 he managed -0.136 EPA per play with the Giants. Nothing in the dossier points to a new skill that explains a jump to 2nd in the league. It does show friendly opponents and a tiny deep sample. Treat 0.321 per dropback as the ceiling of his range, not its center.

concerns.title: Ball security under heat
concerns.body: Two lost fumbles at Las Vegas came in his most pressured-looking game. He held the ball 3.32 seconds and took three sacks after Seattle's tackles went down. The offense already allows hits at a high rate (28th). If he plays behind a line missing its tackles, this is the version to expect, not the clean-pocket one.

concerns.title: Red-zone efficiency is thin
concerns.body: Inside the 20 he has three touchdowns, but those 12 plays carried -0.068 EPA per play. Most of his scoring has come from distance rather than from sustained work in the compressed field. That leaves his touchdown rate (7.5%, 6th) vulnerable to falling back.

trend.note: His last three appearances look almost identical to his season, with EPA per dropback only 0.034 higher. Every logged game was a win against a bottom-ten defense, so the line has been flat largely because the opponent quality has been flat.

nextGame.headline: Darnold's expected return likely sends Lock back to the bench
nextGame.body:
If Lock does play at San Francisco, the matchup is mixed. The 49ers' pass defense is middling (17th in pass EPA). Their pass rush is among the league's weakest (31st in sack rate), and they have lost DT Gracen Halton to IR, all of which would help a passer who thrives with a clean pocket. They are better on the deep ball (4th) and stingy against WR2s, though, which squeezes the shot plays that have fueled his numbers. And their offense ranks 1st in EPA, so a trailing script is a real risk for a QB who has barely played from behind.

Availability decides everything here. Darnold (quadriceps) is listed out but expected back, with his coach optimistic he practices fully after the bye. Lock himself was limited and is listed questionable, and he sits at QB2 on the depth chart. If he were forced in, Charles Cross and Quenton Nelson are out, both every-snap starters, and Abraham Lucas is questionable; all three carry Nov. 29 return estimates. On the other side, CB Renardo Green (back) is questionable, which would open the outside if he sits.

keyMatchups.title: Who starts at quarterback
keyMatchups.body: Darnold is out but listed with a Nov. 29 return, and the coaching staff expects him to start. Lock is the QB2 and carries his own questionable tag. Unless Darnold has a setback, Lock's expected role is the bench.

keyMatchups.title: Patched line vs weak rush
keyMatchups.body: Seattle's starting tackle and guard are out, and the 49ers rank 31st in sack rate. A soft rush partly offsets the line losses, but Las Vegas showed what happens to Lock when protection breaks down.

keyMatchups.title: Deep shots into a sturdy back end
keyMatchups.body: Lock's efficiency rests on deep throws, and San Francisco ranks 4th against them. Expect a shorter, more methodical game if he plays.

nextGame.watch: Darnold's practice status during the bye week: a full week makes Lock a spectator.

restOfSeason.body:
Assume Lock returns to backup duty once Darnold is healthy, which makes his rest-of-season value contingent. If he is pressed into starts, the sustainable parts are the low-turnover approach, the low volume within a run-leaning offense, and the Smith-Njigba connection. The parts that will regress are the deep-ball rate built on nine throws, a touchdown rate propped up by long scores, and efficiency piled up against bottom-tier defenses.

In a start, a realistic line is 170-230 passing yards with one to two touchdowns. EPA per dropback should be closer to average-to-good than to league-best. The weakened offensive line is the biggest threat to that range, and the fumbles at Las Vegas show the downside.
swingFactors: Return of Cross and Nelson to the line

confidence.note: 93 attempts, all against weak defenses, and a role that likely ends with Darnold's return
